name: Fiji

facts.religion: Christian about 64%, Hindu about 28%, Muslim about 6%

snapshot: Sitiveni Rabuka's bid to replace the 2013 constitution split his coalition and forced him to delay a final vote, with an election due by February 2027.
culture: Fiji's iTaukei Indigenous majority and Indo-Fijian community, descended from indentured sugar workers, each keep distinct traditions, from kava ceremonies to Diwali. Rugby sevens is a national obsession; Fiji's Olympic golds in 2016 and 2020 were the country's first medals. Village life, chiefly systems and church on Sunday shape society.
society: Tourism and sugar drive the economy. Tensions between iTaukei and Indo-Fijians led to four coups between 1987 and 2006, the first led by Rabuka himself. Climate change has forced several villages to relocate. Drug trafficking through the Pacific has fuelled a surge in methamphetamine use and HIV.
situation: In 1987, a young lieutenant colonel named Sitiveni Rabuka walked into Fiji's parliament with masked soldiers and overthrew the elected government, the first of two coups he led that year in the name of indigenous Fijian dominance. Thirty-five years later he became prime minister again, this time by winning an election, and has spent his second career trying to cast himself as a reconciler, including backing a truth and reconciliation commission into the coups he himself began. In 2026, as Fiji prepared for an election due by early 2027, the old question came back: can the country move past its military men?

The year was rough for his government. Two deputy prime ministers resigned after being charged by the anti-corruption commission FICAC, one of them Biman Prasad, leader of a coalition partner, prompting claims Rabuka was using the agency against rivals, which he denied (Mai TV). A High Court ruling in favour of the anti-corruption chief he had dismissed embarrassed him further. Opposition figure Savenaca Narube, a former central bank governor, told voters not to "choose military people" to lead again; Rabuka, now 77, replied that Narube did not understand democracy (Fiji Sun). The stakes reach beyond Fiji: Rabuka has pulled the country closer to Australia and away from the Chinese ties his predecessor built.
power: A parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the majority in the 55-seat parliament, elected by open-list proportional representation in a single national constituency; the president, chosen by parliament, is largely ceremonial. The military has historically acted as a political arbiter.
holders: Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka (People's Alliance), leading a three-party coalition since 2022.

update.html: In October parliament advanced the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026, which would replace most of the 2013 constitution while keeping the immunity for past coup makers. Rabuka named 9 December for a referendum, but coalition partner the National Federation Party said it would vote against and SODELPA also objected, leaving him likely short of the 36 votes needed. On 2 November he pushed the committee report back to 30 November, with a final vote expected in early December. Military commander Jone Kalouniwai told parliament the armed forces do not want immunity, and Rabuka said the clause could be dropped. The general election must be held by 6 February 2027.
